use_when: A capable team repeatedly seeks approval for ordinary decisions in the same area of work.
Responsibility for a service or process is broad while authority and neighboring responsibilities remain ambiguous.
A specialist area needs continuing attention and a mandate that survives personnel changes.
goals: Align continuing responsibility with usable authority and means
Reduce repeated approval negotiation for recurring work
Maintain clear boundaries, dependencies, and accountable review
mechanisms: A standing remit identifying purpose, scope, holders, resources, and reserved powers
An authorized delegator with explicit retained and support responsibilities
Agreed interfaces with neighboring domains and internal group decision arrangements
Visible mandate, evidence-based review, and an authorized route to revise or withdraw delegation
example_user_queries: Our team owns a service but needs permission for every ordinary change.
How can we delegate a whole area of work rather than assign one task at a time?
Other departments keep making promises about the work we are responsible for.
What authority and resources should come with owning an ongoing process?
We need a specialist group to maintain an area our leadership cannot attend to in detail.
How do we preserve a team’s mandate when its members change?
Two departments claim control of the same system and nobody knows the boundary.
When should leadership revise a delegation instead of blaming the local team?

visual_decision.reason: Show a continuing area of authority entrusted by a delegator, the holder’s recurring decisions and improvement work, retained review, and distinct relationships with neighboring domains and issues beyond the remit. This explains the mechanism more clearly than an organization chart or decision-by-decision role matrix. Original illustrative arrangement, not a claim about either real example’s exact structure.

sources.basis: Sociocracy 3.0 authors’ primary explanation of domains as responsibility/authority areas, delegation to groups or individuals within constraints, and delegator overall accountability. Used for a short conceptual attribution, not to copy its domain-description template or imply adoption of its complete governance system. The article’s examples, prose, and visual are original synthesis.

Handelsbanken plc’s Annual Report and Financial Statements 2025, printed pages 59–60 (PDF pages 59–60, zero-based 58–59), describes branch-manager or appointed-employee customer and credit responsibility, local decision-making within centralized credit policy, central support, delegated decision limits and controls, and retained central strategy/risk frameworks. Scope is the UK entity and the 2025 reporting period. No unrestricted lending powers, exact lending thresholds, or independent causal performance effects are inferred.

Active primary governance PEP created September 2023 with adoption resolution November 2023: specialist Typing Council mandate, direct smaller specification changes, retained Steering Council authority over overall language direction and PEPs unless separately delegated, accountability, community consultation/public decisions, and no direct authority over external type-checker implementations. Article distinguishes adopted model from the proposal’s hypothetical retrospective examples and does not infer that every such decision happened.

patterns.provenance: Original authority-and-governance synthesis focused on standing authority over a continuing area of work, distinct from Explicit Decision Rights for particular choices and Mission Command for intent-guided adaptation. Museum-network scenario and mechanism diagram are hypothetical. The Handelsbanken example is dated to the UK entity’s 2025 reporting period; Python to the model adopted in 2023, without asserting every proposed illustrative decision occurred or causal benefits were established. S3 supplies a brief acknowledged conceptual connection rather than a copied template or required governance system. No guided practice is created.

patterns.title: Decide Close to the Work
patterns.short_description: Place decisions with the nearest capable people who can understand their effects, supported by clear authority, timely information, and a route for wider issues.
patterns.core_question: Which decisions can people nearest the work make well, and which need a wider view or authority?
use_when: Approval adds delay without adding knowledge to a recurring operational decision.
Conditions change while requests wait for an authority further from the work.
Capable local people can judge the situation if given context, powers, resources, and support.
goals: Locate decision authority near relevant knowledge and feedback
Preserve wider coordination and reserved authority where required
Reduce routine approval queues while strengthening local capability
mechanisms: Decision-category analysis of knowledge, capability, mandate, and affected parties
Usable local authority with explicit resources, controls, and reserved choices
Expert advice and support brought closer without automatically transferring decision ownership
Wider authorization for choices beyond remit, notification of effects, and review of the authority allocation
example_user_queries: Customers wait while our staff ask a distant manager to approve an obvious remedy.
Which operational decisions should move out of headquarters?
The person with approval authority knows less about the situation than the team doing the work.
How can we give local teams more say without making promises that harm neighboring teams?
Our supervisors spend all day approving routine choices instead of handling wider conflicts.
Can an expert help a local team without taking every decision away from it?
When should a frontline decision stay local and when should it escalate?
One delegated decision went badly and leadership wants to take back all local authority.

visual_decision.reason: Show the choice between a supported local decision, bringing in missing expertise, and seeking wider authority. This distinguishes informational support from authorization and explains why proximity alone is insufficient. The three routes are conditional responses, not a serial approval chain. Original mechanism illustration, not either company’s organization chart.

sources.basis: Toyota’s primary overview consulted October 2026 describes an operator stopping the line with a stop cord when an abnormality occurs. Supports a narrow local intervention with wider quality effects, without claiming universal equipment sequences or independently demonstrated productivity benefits.

Official virtual plant tour consulted October 2026 describes a worker pressing a call button to illuminate Andon and inform the leader, with work not resuming until the problem is resolved. Used alongside the overview to retain the combination of local response and support rather than asserting every alert immediately stops every Toyota line.

Timpson’s company account consulted October 2026 gives shop colleagues discretion to serve customers and assigns managers training, tools, support, and mentoring responsibilities. It also states standards and money-handling expectations. Used as documented intended management arrangement, not an exhaustive account of formal authority or independently observed implementation. Numerical compensation allowances and causal performance claims are not inferred.

patterns.provenance: Original authority-and-governance synthesis about choosing the location of authority using knowledge, capability, mandate, and effects. Distinct from Explicit Decision Rights role allocation, Delegated Domains standing remits, Mission Command intent-guided adaptation, and Act Within Your Discretion individual action using existing powers. Equipment-rental scenario and diagram hypothetical. Toyota and Timpson examples are dated to source consultation and described as published arrangements, with limits on implementation consistency and causal performance evidence. No guided practice is created.

patterns.title: Advice Process
patterns.short_description: Require a decision owner to seek and consider advice from affected people and relevant experts, then decide, explain, and remain accountable for the result.
patterns.core_question: How can someone decide independently while learning from the people affected and those with relevant expertise?
use_when: An authorized owner needs knowledge and perspectives distributed across affected people and specialists.
Consultation repeatedly becomes an approval queue or an attempt at unanimous agreement.
Leaders want their experience to inform a decision without taking its ownership away.
goals: Combine clear ownership with meaningful consultation
Separate advice from approval and collective authorization
Make reasons, execution, results, and learning visible
mechanisms: A designated owner whose permission to decide includes a consultation obligation
Advice covering both affected experience and relevant expertise before commitment
Reasoned consideration rather than counting responses or requiring agreement
Communicated decision and reasoning, bounded exception routes, implementation ownership, and result review
example_user_queries: How can I decide without waiting for every stakeholder to agree?
Our decisions miss either the people affected or the technical experts.
A director says they are offering advice but everyone hears an order.
We want colleagues to seek real input without asking the boss for permission.
Can someone reject a recommendation after genuinely consulting the person who gave it?
The same few people are overloaded with requests to comment on proposals.
How do we show that consultation changed a proposal rather than rubber-stamped it?
Who should explain the final choice and follow up when advisers still disagree?

visual_decision.reason: Show two distinct advice constituencies converging on a named owner, followed by communicated reasons, implementation, review, and feedback to advisers. This clarifies obligatory consultation without implied voting or veto rights, while preserving separate required approvals. The original diagram is illustrative rather than either example’s exact procedure.

sources.basis: Dennis Bakke’s primary 7 June 2007 explanation describes an individual decision-maker seeking advice from leaders and peers while retaining the final choice. Used for the core connection between independent ownership and consultation; enjoyment and superior quality claims are identified as practitioner experience rather than comparative evidence. No modern AES practice is inferred.

Company playbook consulted October 2026 specifies advice from affected parties and subject experts and states applicability to UK employees and other business units choosing adoption. Supports the bounded scope rather than claiming uniform adoption throughout the company.

Primary company implementation guide distinguishes self-appointment below thresholds subject to constraints from leadership confirmation for larger commitments. Appointing an owner does not mean approving their eventual outcome; the owner retains responsibility. Article avoids unstable monetary thresholds and generalizing the policy to other organizations.

Primary company guidance favors meaningful conversations, varied representative sampling rather than asking every colleague individually, recording advisers, visible documentation and a period for additional input. Used as one explicit organizational variant, not a universal representation rule or proof of quality.

Henry Stewart’s firsthand company article dated 3 January 2024 describes John and Ben increasing prices through Advice Process despite his preference for a smaller increase, and his subsequent reassessment. Event’s precise date is not given. Article separates the documented ownership/advice arrangement from Stewart’s retrospective suggestion that the change helped survival during the pandemic; no causal conclusion or universal company practice is inferred.

patterns.provenance: Original authority-and-governance synthesis of consultation as an obligation attached to clearly owned decision authority, distinct from consensus, consent, optional suggestion-gathering, and required approvals. Booking-system scenario and diagram hypothetical. Equal Experts is a bounded documented implementation consulted October 2026, including explicit representative consultation; Happy a dated 2024 firsthand retrospective without a precise decision date or independently isolated causal effects. Named co-owners are distinguished from the wider adviser group. No guided practice is created.

patterns.title: Consent Decision-Making
patterns.short_description: Adopt workable proposals when no qualifying objection remains, using reasoned objections to improve the decision and explicit review to learn from it.
patterns.core_question: How can a group decide together without requiring everyone’s preferred option or dismissing serious objections?
use_when: An authorized group needs to adopt a collective policy while accommodating differing preferences.
Majority voting leaves reasoned implementation risks unresolved.
A proposal can be improved and reviewed through clear ownership and meaningful feedback.
goals: Authorize workable collective commitments without requiring everyone’s ideal option
Use reasoned objections to improve proposals before implementation
Preserve clear participation, scope, review, and unresolved-dispute routes
mechanisms: An authorized group with a shared purpose, agreed objection criteria, quorum, and participation rules
Explicit separation of clarification, reactions, and consent checks
Reasoned examination of objections followed by revision and renewed checks
Named implementation owners, review criteria, recorded concerns, and an agreed escalation or deferral route
example_user_queries: Our group keeps searching for an option everyone likes best and never decides.
A proposal wins the vote but a minority still sees a serious implementation risk.
How can we distinguish a personal preference from a reasoned objection?
Can I support trying a proposal even though it is not my preferred solution?
People stop raising concerns because the facilitator treats objections as obstruction.
What should happen when a collective decision has an objection we cannot resolve?
How do we make sure a trial is actually acceptable rather than just calling it safe?
We need clear rules about absent members before treating a committee decision as agreed.

visual_decision.reason: Show a proposal checked for qualifying objections, a separate revision-and-recheck loop, and adoption only when none remain. This distinguishes objection integration from voting or a preference survey and includes the route for an unresolved objection. The original mechanism diagram is not a copied framework procedure or either organization’s precise meeting sequence.

sources.basis: Ted Rau’s primary method explanation, dated 13 July 2022, links sociocratic objections to harm to the circle’s aim, distinguishes preference from consent, and describes explicit consent rounds. Used for a bounded methodological explanation. Broad comparative claims that consensus cannot scale or that autocracy necessarily reduces commitment are not adopted.

Sociocracy 3.0 authors’ primary method page consulted October 2026 includes a broader objection criterion encompassing worthwhile improvements, along with proposal clarification, objection resolution, renewed testing and review. Used briefly to identify real variation across consent methods; article explicitly adopts the narrower purpose/responsibility/implementation-risk focus rather than implying one universal objection definition or copying its full facilitation procedure.

Ted Rau’s firsthand account dated 31 March 2020 of a three-person SoFA support-circle password-consolidation proposal. He describes a negative reaction followed by consent because he judged it workable and supportive of the circle’s administrative aim. Actual meeting date is unspecified. Article does not infer password-security quality, implementation success, or a measured organizational performance benefit.

Equal Care’s primary playbook consulted October 2026 documents consent for most circle decisions and fixed-term role selection, required local quorum/absent-member process, concern monitoring/shorter terms/amendment, referral to a broader circle when unresolved, and explicit exceptions for restructuring and employment-related decisions. Used as organizational governance evidence, not care guidance, legal advice, proof of consistent implementation, or a universal escalation/exception prescription.

patterns.provenance: Original authority-and-governance synthesis focused on collective adoption when no qualifying objection remains, with objections improving the proposal and reviews supporting revision. Explicitly distinguishes varying objection criteria, preferences, majority voting, and Advice Process. Community-workshop opening-hours scenario and mechanism graphic are hypothetical. SoFA example is a dated firsthand retrospective without a precise event date; Equal Care is a published arrangement consulted October 2026. Documented rules and participant interpretations are separated from causal or universal performance evidence. No guided practice is created.

patterns.title: Explicit Escalation Paths
patterns.short_description: Define when an issue needs wider help or authority, who receives it, how responsibility is accepted, and what happens if it remains unresolved.
patterns.core_question: When an issue exceeds ordinary ownership, how does it reach someone equipped to resolve it without being lost between people?
use_when: An issue circulates across units without an accepted owner for the next step.
Conflicting shared commitments exceed local decision authority.
Unavailable recipients or unclear triggers leave requests waiting without a dependable fallback.
goals: Connect unresolved issues to the right expertise, capacity, or authority
Make response and handoff responsibilities observable
Return decisions to implementation and improve recurring structural problems
mechanisms: Recognizable triggers and destinations matched to the missing help or authority
Reachable receiving roles with coverage, alternates, and response expectations
A concise issue account and explicit distinction between receipt, coordination, and decision ownership
Agreed fallback and unresolved-dispute routes, returned outcomes, and review of recurrent escalations
example_user_queries: An urgent problem has been forwarded to five managers but nobody owns the next step.
Who should settle a conflict when two teams have promised the same scarce specialist?
How do people know when to ask for help instead of struggling alone?
Our escalation contact is away and nobody knows who covers them.
A ticket was acknowledged but the underlying issue is still waiting for a decision.
Can we bring in expert help without automatically moving decision authority upward?
People use private escalations to win arguments without showing the competing evidence.
The same issues keep escalating and we need to fix the underlying ownership problem.

visual_decision.reason: Distinguish the issue owner, receiving role, and authorized response, with separate branches for missing acknowledgement and unresolved or out-of-remit issues. The return route makes outcome communication visible and separates receipt from resolution. Original general mechanism, not either example’s precise workflow.

sources.basis: Primary leadership handbook consulted October 2026 describes effective escalation bringing in either an adviser or decision-maker for alignment or serious tradeoffs, suggests a concise account of importance/details/attempts/request, and recognizes exceptions to ordinary notification where raising concerns is unsafe. Used for a brief conceptual distinction, not universal efficacy or a claim that all escalation transfers authority.

Gabe Krabbe’s original Google SRE chapter describes acknowledgement tracking and the Escalator sending to the next configured destination after an interval without acknowledgement, including primary-to-secondary on-call. Article dates the account to the first SRE book and does not infer current Google tooling or that acknowledgement resolves the underlying problem.

Andrea Spadaccini’s original Google SRE chapter describes clear escalation paths, access to partner development teams, and incident-management procedures for multi-team or uncertain-duration incidents. Used for help/coordination beyond notification, without asserting identical rotations across teams or current operational details.
Google Research’s primary publication record establishes O’Reilly publication in 2016. Used solely to date the Google organizational example.

NASA’s primary NPR 7120.5F with Change 4, consulted October 2026, effective date 3 August 2021 and listed expiration 3 February 2027. Section 3.4 requires documented formal dissent, joint facts/positions/impacts/recommendations when time permits, next-authority routing with wider notification, oral urgent presentations with follow-up documentation, returned recorded decisions, and appeal rights up to Administrator. Article describes this bounded space-flight program/project procedure rather than offering legal, engineering, or emergency instructions, and does not infer consistent enforcement or performance outcomes.

patterns.provenance: Original authority-and-governance synthesis of triggers, destinations, response expectations, accepted responsibility, fallback, and closure. Distinct from general decision-right allocation, standing delegation, interpersonal conflict discussion, or incident-management procedures. Design-agency scenario and mechanism graphic are hypothetical. Google practices are dated to the 2016 book; NASA to the consulted F/Change 4 requirements with explicit program/project scope. Published arrangements are separated from current-tooling assumptions and independent evidence of consistent or effective implementation. No guided practice is created.

patterns.title: Integrator Roles
patterns.short_description: Assign a role to reconcile dependencies and tradeoffs across units so their separate contributions form a coherent shared result.
patterns.core_question: Who keeps the whole result coherent when its parts belong to different units?
use_when: Specialist units finish their contributions while the combined product or service fails to fit shared commitments.
Tradeoffs repeatedly cross functions, projects, regions, or partner boundaries.
Coherent delivery needs continuing attention and organizational backing while specialties remain distinct.
goals: Keep a shared result coherent across separately owned contributions
Make dependencies, commitments, and tradeoffs visible and actionable
Preserve specialist ownership and direct collaboration with clear decision routes
mechanisms: A bounded integrator mandate for a product, service, project, or other shared result
Recognized information access, unit counterparts, sponsor support, and explicit decision/escalation powers
A shared view of interfaces and credible commitments negotiated against actual capacity
Direct specialist relationships, end-to-end review, shared records, and acknowledged role handovers
example_user_queries: Every department completes its part but the finished offering still does not work as a whole.
Who should keep product, production, and delivery commitments compatible?
We need someone to reconcile tradeoffs without creating another hidden boss.
Our projects depend on informal favors between departments and nobody owns the whole result.
How can a program lead obtain real commitments from teams they do not manage?
The person coordinating our work is becoming a bottleneck for every conversation.
A local specification change keeps causing unexpected costs in other departments.
Our coordination only works because one person remembers all the relationships and decisions.

visual_decision.reason: Show specialist delivery and direct unit-to-unit connections alongside a named integrator maintaining shared dependencies and tradeoffs. Bidirectional coordination and a separate authority for out-of-mandate choices distinguish this from a reporting chart, ownership integration, or a mandatory communication hub. Furniture-launch illustration is original and hypothetical.

sources.basis: Toyota’s primary 9 April 2012 organizational announcement allocates product-group development responsibility to chief engineers, reinforces technical teams for testing/body/chassis/powertrain and other technologies, places chief engineers under product-planning general managers, and gives chief engineers precedence in design reviews. Article treats this as a historical arrangement/announcement and does not infer detailed staffing rights, absence of direct reports, current structures, or independently established performance effects.

Google’s primary incident-management chapter separates incident command, operational work, communication, and planning. The commander maintains high-level state and a living incident document, structures response responsibilities, removes roadblocks, and explicitly hands over to an acknowledged successor; operations performs system modifications. Used as a bounded integrator-role example rather than generic line authority. The chapter’s fictional worked incident is not represented as an observed case.

Google Research’s primary publication record establishes first publication by O’Reilly in 2016. Supports historical dating of the incident-management account, without assuming current tooling or uniform practice.

patterns.provenance: Original coordination synthesis focused on a recognized role for coherence across separately owned contributions, distinct from Vertical Integration ownership boundaries, Matrix Organization intersecting formal authority, and general dependency coordination techniques. Furniture-launch scenario and diagram are hypothetical. Toyota is a dated 2012 organizational announcement; Google a dated 2016-book arrangement with illustrative narrative explicitly distinguished from observed outcomes. No causal effect or current-structure equivalence is inferred. Creates the previously absent Coordination Across Boundaries collection and links it from the existing verse using established strict metadata and wiki-link conventions. No guided practice is created.

patterns.title: Double Linking
patterns.short_description: Connect two groups through two distinct people who participate in governance decisions in both.
patterns.core_question: How can connected groups influence each other’s decisions without depending on one person to speak for both?
use_when: A leader is the sole interpreter of a group’s concerns in a coordinating body.
Autonomous groups need continuing representation in decisions affecting their domains or resources.
Interdependent peer groups need reciprocal influence beyond occasional consultation.
goals: Provide reciprocal participation in governance across a group boundary
Keep representation from depending on a single person
Preserve separate domains while connecting their decisions
mechanisms: Two distinct people hold overlapping governance membership in two connected groups
Clear selection, confirmation, term, replacement, and accountability arrangements give each connection legitimacy
Both links bring context into deliberation with recognized participation rights rather than reporting alone
Accessible records, defined domains, absence cover, and explicit exceptions keep representation workable
example_user_queries: Our team leader is the only person who gets to explain our concerns to the central group.
How can local units have a real voice in decisions made by the coordinating body?
Information travels between departments but neither can influence the other’s policies.
We hear about decisions after they are settled and cannot shape them beforehand.
One person speaks for both sides whenever our teams disagree.
How do we connect autonomous groups without merging their responsibilities?
Our representative attends meetings but is only allowed to report and leave.
We need more than one route for local concerns to reach wider governance.

visual_decision.reason: Overlapping group frames with two distinct shared participants clarify that the mechanism is membership in both decision processes, rather than two directional reporting arrows. The original hypothetical peer arrangement shows one representative selected by each circle; nested leader/delegate selection rules are explicitly identified as variants.

sources.basis: Primary Sociocracy 3.0 authors’ definition: two interdependent teams each select a member to represent their interests in the other team’s governance decisions. Supports the peer variant and two-way influence. Original explanatory synthesis and geometry rather than reproduction of the source’s phrasing or image.

SCCAN’s primary How We Work + Purposes for Circles v5, December 2022, pages 2–3. Working-circle domains, General Circle coordination, Lead Link and Delegate membership in both circles and consent rights in each. Used as a dated published organizational arrangement; no endorsement of the document’s stronger assertion that structure eliminates power-over, no present-day structure or measured performance inferred.

Sociocracy For All’s primary governance agreement published 28 July 2021, section B. Leader selection/reciprocal confirmation, subcircle-selected parent-confirmed delegates, full membership in both circles, consent policy decisions, and optional single linking with an on-call delegate at more focused levels. A dated governance provision, not evidence of implementation fidelity or performance improvement.

patterns.provenance: Original coordination synthesis focused on two distinct shared governance members across a boundary, with peer and nested variants distinguished. Not a generic information channel, an additional manager, a whole sociocratic system, or a substitute for clear domains. Opening cooperative scenario and explanatory diagram are hypothetical. SCCAN and Sociocracy For All examples are dated primary governance documents; structural implications are separated from verified implementation and causal benefits. Existing collection, verse, strict public metadata, and wiki-link conventions reused. No guided practice created.

patterns.title: Liaison Networks
patterns.short_description: Connect units through named contacts who exchange context, route questions, and maintain working relationships.
patterns.core_question: How can separate units keep useful working connections without relying on personal favors or escalating every question?
use_when: People struggle to find a dependable counterpart for recurring issues across units.
Guidance and changes cross unit boundaries without enough context or timely local feedback.
Coordination depends on personal relationships that disappear when people change roles.
goals: Make cross-unit counterparts and working interfaces dependable
Carry context in both directions and close loops on questions
Preserve unit ownership and direct specialist relationships
mechanisms: Named local contacts with a bounded scope, credible access, cover, and explicit role succession
A maintained directory and suitable communication rhythm linking peers or local contacts with a coordinating function
Clear distinctions between informing, convening, negotiating, and approving decisions
Protected time, orientation, shared follow-up records, direct relationships, and fallback to authorized owners
example_user_queries: Nobody knows who to ask in another department when a recurring issue comes up.
Our coordination depends on personal favors and breaks down when someone leaves.
Central announcements reach local teams but nobody explains what they mean for our work.
Changes at one site reach other sites after they have already made their plans.
We need dependable contacts across units without creating another management layer.
Our named representatives forward messages but never check whether anyone answered.
How can local teams send practical concerns back to a central specialist function?
Every question between departments ends up going through senior management.

visual_decision.reason: Three separate units retain delivery and decision ownership while named contacts inside them connect through questions, context, and follow-up. The original illustrative peer network distinguishes maintained working connections from reporting lines, compulsory message relays, combined-result ownership, and Double Linking governance membership. Central specialist coordination is explained as another configuration rather than depicted as a new boss.

sources.basis: CERN primary account by its Director for International Relations dated 13 March 2017. Describes formalizing senior personnel as Management Liaisons for Member States with proactive dialogue mandates, coordinated by the Member State Relations Section, and forming a network supporting communication, high-level visits, and compatriot community building. The article dates the arrangement and identifies CERN’s effectiveness assessment as self-report; it does not assume present staffing, claim a particular contact cadence, or infer measured causal benefits.

Adobe primary Trust Center description consulted 29 October 2026. Describes an advanced-security-trained engineer embedded as security champion in each product team, communicating security priorities and helping completion, with close Adobe Security connections, regular updates, communications, and training. Used as a distributed specialist-interface arrangement, not a claim of independently verified team coverage, peer meeting cadence, bidirectional feedback processes, approval rights, or security performance improvement.

patterns.provenance: Original synthesis of maintained cross-unit working interfaces through named local contacts, supported mandates, relationships, and follow-up. Standard spelling Liaison Networks used for the user’s Liasison Networks request. Distinct from shared governance membership, an integrator’s combined-result accountability, informal helpful relationships, and compulsory gatekeeping. Museum scenario and peer-network graphic are hypothetical. CERN’s example is dated March 2017; Adobe’s self-description is qualified by consultation date and does not independently establish implementation or effects. Existing collection, strict metadata, wiki links, and asset conventions reused. No guided practice created.

patterns.title: Boundary Objects
patterns.short_description: Coordinate through shared artifacts that remain recognizable across groups while supporting their different uses.
patterns.core_question: How can groups coordinate around the same work when they need to understand it differently?
use_when: Groups use the same terms for different events or omit information needed at handovers.
Specialists need different local detail while coordinating around shared stages or interfaces.
Cross-unit choices rely on disconnected representations and knowledge held in people’s memories.
goals: Provide a recognizable common reference across different working perspectives
Preserve useful local detail while exposing mismatches at boundaries
Connect shared representations to stewardship, authority, and change processes
mechanisms: A shared artifact anchored in an actual crossing of work between groups
Enough stable structure to preserve identity alongside flexible local views and annotations
Active use in reviews and handovers to surface differences and clarify consequential meanings
Named stewardship, content owners, decision rights, version continuity, and explicit unresolved points
example_user_queries: Our departments describe the same service differently and keep missing handovers.
Everyone uses the same words but they mean different things in different teams.
How can specialists coordinate without forcing everyone to use one department’s entire model?
We have plenty of shared documents but they do not help people work together.
Our customer journey, operational process, and financial controls never line up.
Each team has its own spreadsheet and we cannot tell whether they describe the same thing.
How can we keep useful local detail while agreeing the interfaces between our work?
A map looks agreed in meetings but nobody knows who owns its assumptions or changes.

visual_decision.reason: One hypothetical returns map connects three groups with different local concerns while preserving common Requested, Received, and Refunded stages. Bidirectional links distinguish working through and contributing to a shared reference from a one-way broadcast. The diagram clarifies the stable shared identity/local usefulness mechanism without reproducing the museum study’s imagery or implying NASA affiliation.

sources.basis: Original research by Susan Leigh Star and James R. Griesemer, Social Studies of Science 19(3), August 1989, pages 387–420, analyzing Berkeley Museum of Vertebrate Zoology work in 1907–1939. Establishes the concept’s origin, shared identity with different local uses, and historical case scope. Article is an original editorial application, not a reproduction of the authors’ typology or source wording.

Author-hosted copy of the same primary study. Pages 410–411 describe California maps with shared state boundaries but collector/conservationist trail and location detail versus biologists’ life zones, and standardized collecting forms across dispersed sites. Text was cross-checked against the searchable University of Udine-hosted copy of the identical paper because the author-hosted PDF returned no extractable lines. Historical mechanisms are attributed to the original authors’ analysis, not represented as current museum arrangements or universal causal proof.

NASA primary Systems Engineering Handbook interface-management guidance consulted 29 October 2026. Describes divided development across government, contractors, and geographically separated technical teams; interface control documentation and approved change management. Used as a documented organizational coordination design, not an observed mission case or NASA’s own application of the Boundary Objects label.

NASA primary interface-requirements outline, section 1.3 assigning participating organizations’ document-development responsibilities, approval authority, and change authority. Supports explicit stewardship/authority in the NASA example without offering engineering instructions or implying that a shared artifact settles authority by itself.

patterns.provenance: Original coordination synthesis of stable common references, differing local uses, active working practices, stewardship, and decision rights. Distinct from mere document access, uniform interpretation, generic visualization, or authority inferred from a diagram. Retail returns scenario and explanatory SVG are hypothetical. Museum example is explicitly the 1907–1939 historical case interpreted in the 1989 primary study. NASA example is a published coordination procedure, with Boundary Objects identified as this article’s interpretation and no mission-performance claim. Existing collection, verse, strict public metadata, wiki links, and visual system reused. No guided practice created.

patterns.title: Dependency Mapping
patterns.short_description: Make cross-unit dependencies explicit so people can see prerequisites, shared constraints, and the consequences of change.
patterns.core_question: What does each unit depend on, and where could one change disrupt the wider work?
use_when: Local progress reports obscure relationships that determine whether a shared result can proceed.
A change may propagate across teams, services, suppliers, or partners that its owner cannot identify confidently.
Several initiatives share scarce inputs or capabilities and leaders need to examine coordination or redesign.
goals: Expose the network of reliance across organizational boundaries
Trace upstream prerequisites and downstream consequences without treating assumptions as commitments
Connect shared constraints and changes to authorized decisions and work redesign
mechanisms: A bounded map of recognizable contributions or capabilities with responsible units and explicit connection meanings
Validation at both ends, including usable inputs, necessary versus assumed relationships, and visible uncertainty
Upstream/downstream tracing, converging inputs, shared prerequisites, cycles, and separately identified resource competition
Named map stewardship, local commitment authority, change review, escalation, and retirement of obsolete connections
example_user_queries: Every team reports progress but we cannot see what the whole launch is waiting for.
How do we find out which other units will be affected if this contribution slips?
Several initiatives rely on the same specialist and their local plans all look feasible.
Our organization chart tells us who reports to whom but not who needs what from whom.
We need a shared picture of prerequisites that does not turn requested dates into promises.
People keep discovering upstream requirements after they have started dependent work.
How can we identify recurring dependencies that make our organizational boundaries costly?
Our services rely on other services and suppliers, but nobody understands the wider exposure.

visual_decision.reason: An original hypothetical housing-association pilot shows one procurement prerequisite fanning out to operations and service-desk work, with both feeding pilot readiness. Explicit prerequisite-to-dependent arrows and an unconfirmed status reveal cross-unit consequences without implying reporting relationships, commitments, duration estimates, or a calculated critical path.

sources.basis: Atlassian primary Team Playbook guidance consulted 29 October 2026. Identifies upstream/downstream affected systems, owners, impacts, risks, mitigation responsibility, feedback cadence, adjacent-team review, and continued map updates. Used briefly as practitioner-method support, not as proof of improved outcomes or as a reproduction of its worksheet or workshop procedure.

National Audit Office primary investigation dated 3 May 2019, paragraphs 2.24–2.27. Found Crossrail’s handover schedule lacked sufficient bottom-up integration, logical sequencing, cross-contract dependencies, and an effective tool for completion-risk decisions. Provides dated independent audit context, not proof that mapping is the sole cause of delivery performance.

Delivery participant WSP’s primary account dated 16 September 2022, describing an SI team mobilized in early 2019 and a single-page migration plan connecting milestone logic, railway capability stages, signalling, rolling stock, stations, and the route toward May 2022 opening. Used as a dated firsthand organizational example; promotional assertions of universal success, precise critical-path certainty, and mapping-only causation are not adopted.

Government Office for Science primary blog by Lizzie Greenhaigh and Joe Randall dated 12 July 2018. Describes Policy Lab/UK Space Agency collaboration on an interactive dependency map connecting critical national infrastructure with space services, informed by the GNSS review and driver-mapping techniques, used for stakeholder engagement. Reports stakeholder understanding, not measured resilience improvement; current maintenance or use is not inferred.

patterns.provenance: Original organizational coordination synthesis focused on a cross-unit network of reliance, propagation, shared constraints, and uncertainty. Existing Coordinate Dependencies Early article inspected and retained as a related broader handoff-agreement pattern; this article’s distinct focus is the map and the network-level questions it supports. Distinguishes sequence, continuing service reliance, and competition for capacity, with no critical-path claim absent durations and validated logic. Housing-association scenario and mechanism diagram are hypothetical. Crossrail is bounded by the 2019 audit and 2022 participant account; UKSA/Policy Lab by the 2018 government account. Current practices and causal performance effects are not inferred. Existing collection, strict metadata, references, and visual conventions reused. No guided practice created.

patterns.title: Team API
patterns.short_description: Make a team’s responsibilities, offerings, and interaction expectations explicit and easy for other teams to use.
patterns.core_question: How can other teams know what we own, what we offer, and how to work with us?
use_when: People need personal introductions to discover ownership, available offerings, or how to request help.
Scattered request channels produce conflicting promises, invisible work, or confusion about response versus acceptance.
Team relationships are changing and neighboring teams need a usable description of responsibilities and interaction modes.
goals: Make the team’s external working interface discoverable and usable
Align supported offerings, routes, and expectations with actual capacity and authority
Keep interaction descriptions current while preserving accessible human conversations
mechanisms: A maintained outward-facing description of purpose, ownership, usable offerings, and significant boundaries
Clear routes for routine requests, questions, joint work, incidents, and exceptions with suitable entry information
Distinctions among acknowledgment, assessment, acceptance, scheduling, and completion, with credible priority and capacity rules
Important partner relationships and modes, named maintenance, user feedback, and links to authorized decisions
example_user_queries: How do other departments find out what our team owns and how to work with us?
